newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung vague on fate of democrat councillors.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung vague on fate of democrat councillors.

text.p: China's hand-picked leader for Hong Kong, Tung Chee-hwa, who supports curbs on civil liberties, left the fate of elected local councillors in doubt on Monday after failing to guarantee their seats under Chinese rule.

Elected members of the Urban Council, Regional Council and District Boards, which play a major role in local government, have been fretting about their future as China unveiled plans in recent months to whittle down Hong Kong's fledgling democracy.

Tung's meeting with members of the Urban Council was the latest in a series of negative signals on the future of human rights and democracy after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
A week ago the China-controlled Preparatory Committee, which is crafting Hong Kong's new political arrangements, approved a plan to replace the present local councils.
Tung, who co-chairs the Preparatory Committee, refused to promise that all incumbent urban councillors would be allowed to serve beyond the mid-1997 handover.
Democratic Party councillor Fred Li said he was dismayed that Tung had refused to directly answer questions about the future of pro-democracy members when he met them on Monday.
"He didn't particularly answer the question which those Democratic Party members asked...whether they will go through. He didn't answer the question," Li told reporters.

"Mr Tung always repeats the same old comment, that we need stability, we need a smooth transition, we don't want to see too many political disputes, arguments, in the Urban Council, in society as a whole," Li said.
Britain is handing back the territory of 6.3 million people under a 1984 treaty, amid growing signs there will be major political changes after the red flag of China is hoisted.
Tung will be its chief executive, replacing colonial Governor Chris Patten, and the post-colonial leader chosen by China has unswervingly echoed Beijing's tough line.

He has thrown his weight behind a Chinese plan to replace Hong Kong's democratically-elected Legislative Council with an appointed shadow legislature and to repeal key parts of the Bill of Rights and laws on elections and political freedoms.
The Democratic Party, the largest force in legislative elections in 1995, is excluded from the new legislature.

Under the proposals of the Preparatory Committee, Tung will expand membership of the local councils by 25 percent by appointing additional members. Serving members are expected to stay on but Tung will have the final say on who remains.
Urban Council chairman Ronald Leung said after Monday's meeting that Tung promised to consult widely before deciding.
"What he said was that he would consult the various opinions widely, and especially would respect the opinions expressed by the urban councillors," Leung said.

Leung said Tung had told the councillors he would deliberate on the issue in his advisory cabinet, the Executive Council, before submitting a proposal to the shadow legislature, which holds its meetings over the border in China's Shenzhen city.
